title: The Partner Revenue Readiness Score
subtitle: Find out whether your channel marketing is planting seeds for a long-term harvest — or scrambling at year-end.

questions.text: When does your team start building partner revenue plans for the coming year?

answers.label: We react to targets when they arrive — usually Q4 or later
We start planning in Q3 but it is rushed and often incomplete
We begin in Q2 with some forward visibility but no formal cycle
We run a structured planning cycle starting at least 12 months out
We run rolling 18-month plans and review them every quarter

questions.text: How would you describe your Q3 and Q4 each year?

answers.label: Stressful — we are always chasing the number with no clear plan
Busy and reactive — lots of last-minute activity to close gaps
Moderately controlled — we have a plan but still face surprises
Well-managed — we know roughly where we will land and are already thinking about next year
Calm and confident — our harvest reflects seeds planted 12 months ago

questions.text: How clearly can you trace today's partner marketing activity to a specific revenue target 12 months from now?

answers.label: We cannot — activity and targets are managed separately
We have a rough sense but no formal link between activity and future targets
Some programmes tie to future targets; others do not
Most activity maps to specific targets with clear milestones
Every programme has a named pipeline owner, a revenue target, and a review date

questions.text: How many hours per week does your team spend on reactive partner requests or ad-hoc work — rather than planned strategic activity?
questions.hint: Be honest — this includes last-minute briefs, unplanned campaigns, and chasing approvals. We'll show you the annual cost of this across 52 working weeks.

low.headline: You're firefighting, not farming.
low.text: The year-end panic is a symptom, not the problem. The real problem is that revenue planning is reactive — which means the seeds for next year's harvest are not being planted right now. Forward-thinking partner teams are not scrambling in Q4 because they had a plan in Q2 of the year before.
steps: Block time in the next four weeks to map the partner marketing activity you need to run in the coming 12 months against your revenue targets — even a rough plan beats none at all
Assign a named owner to each planned programme with a pipeline number attached, not just an activity metric
Set a quarterly review date now so you are adapting before the panic sets in, not after

mid.headline: You're starting to think like a farmer — but there are gaps in the plan.
mid.text: You are ahead of most. But if Q3 and Q4 still feel rushed, the planning cycle has a leak somewhere — in the initial target-setting, the programme design, or the review cadence. Finding where it breaks is the most valuable thing you can do this quarter.
steps: Look at the last three years of Q4 performance: when did you know whether you would hit the number, and why? That moment usually reveals exactly where the plan broke down
Tighten the link between partner marketing activity and pipeline reporting so leadership can see the connection — that visibility protects your budget when it matters most
Bring your top partners into planning conversations earlier — they have market timing insight you are probably not using yet

high.headline: You're running a well-tended harvest. Now protect the plan.
high.text: Strong planning discipline puts you in a small minority of channel teams. The risk at this stage is not falling behind — it is that a strategy built for last year's market has not evolved with your partners' changing needs.
steps: Run an annual audit of your top partners: are they still the right ones to invest in, or has the market shifted around them?
Build contingency into your plans so a single partner underperforming does not blow your year
The best channel teams pull partners into strategy conversations, not just execution — if you are not doing this yet, start there

questions.text: How would you describe your approach to claiming MDF each quarter?

answers.label: We rarely claim it — the process is unclear and the admin feels like too much effort
We claim some, but often leave money on the table by the quarter's end
We claim most of it, but mainly for the same types of activity each time
We have a consistent claiming process and plan activity against the budget in advance
MDF is fully integrated into our annual marketing plan with defined programmes and ROI tracking

questions.text: When you use MDF, how is the activity designed?

answers.label: We pick something quick that is easy to get approved — usually events or branded collateral
We run whatever the vendor suggests without always linking it to our own pipeline goals
We pitch activities that work for both sides, though the strategy varies by programme
Activities are chosen to serve a specific pipeline or audience goal agreed with the vendor upfront
Every MDF programme has a defined audience, a revenue target, and a review date agreed before a penny is spent

questions.text: How do you measure the return on MDF-funded activity?

answers.label: We do not track it beyond submitting the claim form
We track attendance or outputs such as leads generated, but not revenue impact
We track influenced pipeline but it is not always tied back to the specific MDF programme
We track leads, pipeline, and closed revenue per programme and report this to the vendor
ROI data from each programme informs the next planning cycle and strengthens our case for future MDF allocation

questions.text: What percentage of your available MDF do you typically claim and spend each quarter?
questions.hint: Industry data suggests around 60% of MDF goes unclaimed every quarter. Enter your honest number — this feeds your results.

low.headline: 60% of MDF goes unclaimed every quarter. Don't let yours add to that number.
low.text: MDF is sales opportunity support — and if you are not claiming it, you are effectively funding other partners' growth. The admin feels like the barrier, but the real barrier is not having a plan to use it strategically. That is fixable in one conversation with your vendor rep.
steps: Book a call this month specifically to understand what MDF you have available and what activities qualify — most vendors want to spend it and simply need someone to show up with a plan
Draft a 90-day plan for two or three activities tied to a specific pipeline target and bring it to that conversation — partners who arrive with a plan get funded first
Start tracking outputs from every MDF activity, even informally: leads, meetings, pipeline influenced. That data is what gets you more next quarter

mid.headline: You're using MDF. Now make it work much harder.
mid.text: Claiming MDF for the sake of it does not build your business. The teams I see getting the most out of it treat it like investment capital: specific activity, specific audience, specific outcome. If your vendor cannot see a clear ROI story in your reporting, you are at risk of losing budget to partners who can.
steps: Review your last three MDF-funded programmes: what pipeline did they create? Which performed best and why?
Shift at least one upcoming programme to a targeted approach — a defined list of accounts rather than a broad campaign
Build a one-page ROI template for every programme so vendor reporting becomes fast and your case for future MDF gets stronger each quarter

high.headline: You're treating MDF like investment capital. That's exactly right.
high.text: Strong utilisation with solid ROI reporting puts you in a position to ask for more budget — and get it. The next move is using that data to influence vendor planning cycles, not just react to them.
steps: Take your ROI data into your next vendor QBR and open a conversation about co-planning next year's MDF allocation — not just claiming what is given
Identify the one or two programmes that consistently outperform and build a repeatable playbook around them
Consider sharing your approach publicly — an article or talk on making MDF work builds your profile with both prospects and vendors, and most people in the channel never do it

questions.text: How clearly defined is your (or your partners') unique value proposition in the market?

answers.label: We have not formally defined one — we describe what we do, not why we are different
We have something written down but it sounds like every other partner in our space
We have a value proposition but it does not consistently appear in our marketing or sales conversations
Our value proposition is clear, differentiated, and understood by the sales team
Our value proposition is specific, evidenced with customer proof, and used consistently across all channels

questions.text: If a prospect asked your best salesperson 'why should I choose you over the other three resellers I'm talking to?' — what would happen?

answers.label: They would lead with price or the vendor's product features — not what makes us different
They would say something reasonable but it would differ from what a colleague would say
There is a consistent answer but it is still feature-focused rather than outcome-led
They would give a clear, differentiated answer grounded in our track record and specific to the prospect's situation
They would tell a compelling, consistent story with proof points specific to that prospect's world — and every salesperson would tell the same story

questions.text: How does your marketing communicate what makes you (or your partners) genuinely different from the competition?

answers.label: Most of it is vendor-branded content we have repurposed — our own voice is largely absent
We produce some original content but it focuses on product features rather than our specific expertise
We have original content that reflects our expertise but it is inconsistent and does not always connect to pipeline
Our marketing consistently reflects our positioning and drives conversations with the right types of buyers
Our content, campaigns, and sales materials all reinforce a clear point of view that our target customers recognise and respond to

low.headline: If your customers can't articulate why they chose you, your marketing hasn't done its job.
low.text: In a crowded channel, the partners who win are not always the ones with the best product access — they are the ones who can articulate their own value most clearly. Relying on vendor content and product specs means you are competing on price, not on what makes you genuinely worth choosing.
steps: Talk to two or three of your best customers this week: ask them why they chose you and what would happen if you were not there. Write down exactly what they say — that is your value proposition draft
Audit your last ten pieces of marketing content: how much is vendor material versus your own point of view? Set a target to shift the balance over the next quarter
Write one piece of content this month that only you could have written — a specific client outcome, a decision you made, a view on your market that is genuinely yours

mid.headline: You know what makes you different. Now make sure your market does too.
mid.text: Having a clear value proposition internally is the starting point, not the finish line. The gap I see most often is consistency — how reliably it shows up in conversations, in content, and in how your team talks about you when you are not in the room.
steps: Create a one-page 'why us' document for your salespeople — not a corporate deck, but a straight answer to the question prospects ask most often
Take your strongest customer story and turn it into three formats: a reference call offer, a written case study, and a social post. One story, three sales tools
Test your value proposition with a prospect who does not know you well — does it land clearly, or does it need sharpening?

high.headline: Strong positioning is a competitive advantage. Now scale it.
high.text: Clear, consistent, evidenced positioning is genuinely rare in the channel. You have done the hard work — the opportunity now is making sure it reaches the right people at the right scale.
steps: Map your value proposition to specific buyer personas: does it land equally well with IT directors, finance leads, and ops managers, or does it need nuancing by audience?
Use your strongest proof points as the foundation for an ABM programme targeting the accounts where your positioning is most compelling
Consider whether your positioning could also attract better talent — the best people want to work for businesses with a clear point of view

questions.text: How targeted is your partner marketing activity — as a vendor investing in partners, or as a partner investing in your own pipeline?

answers.label: Mostly broad — we campaign to the widest audience possible and hope the right people respond
We segment by industry or company size but do not work from named account lists
We work with some named account lists but ABM is applied inconsistently
We have a defined tiered account list and tailor content and outreach to specific accounts or segments
ABM is central to our approach — every major programme is built around named accounts with specific outcomes

questions.text: How aligned are your marketing and sales teams around which accounts to target?

answers.label: Marketing and sales operate independently — there is no shared account list
There is some overlap but marketing and sales are often pursuing different audiences
We align quarterly but day-to-day execution still drifts apart
Marketing and sales share the same account list and review it together at least monthly
Marketing, sales, and the vendor partner team are fully aligned on target accounts with a shared pipeline view

questions.text: How do you decide which accounts deserve the most marketing investment?

answers.label: Budget tends to follow the most noise or urgency — there is no formal process
We use gut instinct or whichever accounts are most active on our list
We use some scoring criteria such as size, sector, or fit — but not consistently
We have a scoring model that tiers accounts by potential and budget allocation follows it
We score accounts on fit, potential, and intent data — investment decisions are driven by that model and reviewed regularly

questions.text: When a vendor offers you marketing support or co-investment, how do you respond?

answers.label: We take what is offered and run it as given, without shaping it to our audience or pipeline
We adapt the materials slightly but run the campaign broadly as the vendor designed it
We use the vendor's framework but overlay our own customer insight and targeting
We co-plan campaigns with the vendor from the start, bringing our own account data and pipeline context
We have a standing process for vendor co-marketing that starts with our accounts and pipeline, not the vendor's calendar

low.headline: Fishing with a net in a sea of noise isn't a strategy. It's hope.
low.text: Broad campaigns feel productive because they generate activity. But in the channel, the highest-returning marketing I see is almost always the most targeted. ABM for partners is still under-used — which means there is a real advantage for the teams who get it right first.
steps: Start small: ask your top three salespeople to name their ten most important target accounts each. That combined list of thirty is your first ABM tier — start there this quarter
Run one campaign exclusively for those named accounts — personalised, specific, and tightly followed up by sales
Measure the difference in engagement and pipeline between that targeted activity and your next broad campaign, and let the numbers make the case internally

mid.headline: You're doing some targeting. Now make it systematic.
mid.text: The jump from 'we do some ABM' to 'ABM is how we run our channel' comes from consistency. Named account lists, regular marketing and sales alignment, and a clear view of which accounts move and why — that is where the revenue lives.
steps: Formalise your account tiering: Tier 1 strategic and high-touch, Tier 2 growth and programmatic, Tier 3 nurture and light touch — and make sure budget allocation actually reflects that split
Add a monthly marketing and sales alignment meeting with one standing agenda item: which accounts moved, which did not, and what are we changing?
Ask your vendor partner manager about overlaying their intent data or install base with your account list — most vendors have this; most partners never ask for it

high.headline: You're using ABM properly. Now use it to pull better investment from your vendors.
high.text: A mature ABM approach with named accounts and pipeline data is the strongest possible case for vendor co-investment. You are in a position most channel marketers are not — the move now is making sure your vendors know it.
steps: Take your account data and pipeline model into your next vendor QBR and use it to negotiate co-investment in your top accounts — come with the numbers, not just the ask
Look at whether ABM techniques could extend to partner recruitment: are you targeting the right new partners with the same rigour you apply to customers?
Consider publishing a point of view on ABM for partners in your market — you have real experience, and most people in the channel are still figuring it out

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: Most people don't fail at the assessment. They fail at sequencing. In 30 minutes I'll show you which two things to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing call.

computed_outputs.label: Hours lost to reactive work per year
